facts: Mark's conflicts with particular Jewish leaders cannot authorize antisemitism, supersessionism, deicide accusations, collective Jewish guilt, or portraying Pharisees and Judaism as uniquely hypocritical, impure, or hard-hearted.

Prevents opening the passage as though the accusation concerned eating a prohibited animal.
Mark contrasts ingested material entering stomach rather than heart with harmful acts proceeding from within.

Workshop caves and production debris at Reina, approximately three kilometers from Nazareth, attest regional manufacture of soft-limestone vessels used in Jewish settlements.
The workshops show that stone vessels associated with purity practice were locally available, contextualizing John 2 and purity disputes without identifying the Cana jars or Mark's opponents.
Six fragmentary Cave 4 manuscripts preserve portions of a reconstructed work addressing calendar and legal matters and explaining separation based on disputed practices.

4QMMT demonstrates that detailed Torah and purity disagreements could mark communal boundaries before the New Testament period without making its authors the unnamed background of any one Gospel or Acts dispute.
Josephus distinguishes three Jewish groups and assigns them different views or practices concerning law, providence, fate, afterlife, authority, and communal discipline.
His descriptions supply later-composed context for the Pharisee-Sadducee disagreement in Acts 23 while preserving the possibility that Luke and Josephus frame the groups differently.
Mark, Acts, Romans, and First Corinthians organize food and purity around different disputes, actors, settings, and outcomes.

Leviticus assigns different causes, durations, rites, access effects, and sanctions to bodily impurity and prohibited conduct.
Prevents later clean and unclean language from becoming personal guilt, dirtiness, or diminished human worth.
Katharizon panta ta bromata admits competing analyses with different implications for hand-defiled food and Torah food distinctions.
Mark preserves and translates several Semitic expressions, including Boanerges, Talitha koum, Corban, Ephphatha, Bartimaeus, Abba, Golgotha, and Eloi.

Mark's healing stories portray embodied need and restored participation, yet cure-centered reception can stigmatize disabled people and must not equate bodily difference with sin, weak faith, or spiritual failure.
The grammar and scope of Mark 7:19 remain disputed; readings range from an editorial declaration about all foods to an anatomical claim about digestion that does not repeal kashrut.
Mark's Sabbath, handwashing, purity, divorce, commandment, and temple disputes are intrajewish arguments in a Jewish scriptural world, not evidence that Judaism was uniquely legalistic.
Rome, Syria, Galilee, and other settings have been proposed, but no city or single ethnic audience can be established from the text.
The Syrophoenician woman answers Jesus' children-and-dogs saying and obtains her daughter's release; interpretations of testing, boundary, ethnicity, gender, and change remain disputed.
